items.title: tech is the bottleneck
items.summary:
humanity usually doesn't solve its problems through coordination. we know many solutions and yet, it takes a new technology. getting people to change their behavior or act in concert is hard. it usually only happens through a shared higher purpose. as society is getting so complex for our little brain that finding a joint higher purpose is difficult. and for many, even finding a personal higher purpose is becoming harder. 

the way forward is achieved by tinkering in public. and tinkering is, as proto-industrial britain shows, largely a question of perceived security. people need not to worry about failing. to grant due status to those who test hypotheses until they succeed, we need to weave a shared narrative. that narrative shift will likely be achieved through educational and communication tech that helps every individual understand more complexity and speak their truth constructively.
items.grounded: → why i co-founded a think tank that builds trust networks between diplomats, ai labs, and researchers across geopolitical fault-lines.

items.title: bounded rationality
items.summary: humans rarely optimize but satisfice. we decide with incomplete information, finite time, and limited compute. kahneman treats this as systematic error to be corrected. gigerenzer gets closer: heuristics are adaptive compressions, not bugs to fix. 'correcting' one bias means degrading performance somewhere else in the system. you can find better compressions — better heuristics — but you can't magically debias your way to optimality. two people with identical values will pursue different approaches because they're working from different slices of reality.
items.grounded: → why policymakers aren't able to feel the stakes of agi and why i advocate for people causing more friction to hash things out in detail.

items.title: everything should be thinkable
items.summary: no idea should be off-limits for consideration. the moment you declare a thought unthinkable, you lose the ability to reason about it — and reasoning about hard things is exactly how you avoid the worst outcomes. this is not the same as saying everything should be done. thinking is not endorsing. keeping everything publicly thinkable is precisely how you prevent dangerous ideas from festering underground. the defense against bad-faith exploitation is raising the bar for morally acceptable behavior and holding each other accountable to that in action, rather than policing thoughts.
items.grounded: → why i treasure invite-only communities and twitter anons.

items.title: language is coordination infrastructure
items.summary: language is our highest-bandwidth tool, and many cultures use it ineffectively. better norms can compress more information and multiply collective intelligence. writing and programming both train this skill: forcing us to compress thoughts into scrutinizable form. the bottleneck of inter-brain communication might be what made us smart in the first place and we can wield it ever better.
items.grounded: → why i believe that most expectations of fundamental value divergences are mostly just failures  in bridging inferential distance.

items.title: the uncanny valley of improvement
items.summary: to get from one local optimum to a better one, things often get worse temporarily. the art is being fine with this. e.g. when learning something, you will temporarily feel more stupid than before starting to dig in but eventually a better full picture emerges. or in game theoretic terms, moving from hunting hare (everyone traps one for themselves -- easy but mediocre) to stag hunting (coordinated chase -- difficult but high payoff) means tolerating an occasional error — coordination skills and infrastructure are a fail-forward exercise. depending on the scale of change, the discomfort might last a good while. we need to tolerate this for ourselves and also for others. normalize ambitious tinkering, cushion the falls, and make striving appreciated. accepting where we're at is important -- as long as we also repeatedly attempt to push further.
items.grounded: → a lesson i learned way too late myself. why i am trying to support more entrepreneurship and try to push people to think beyond individual contributions. also a key difficulty in policy work, or when changing a user experience. often, we can only explain to a small minority and have to sit out the rest of the complaints.

items.title: trust but verify & focusing on what you want to see more of
items.summary: we're walking a tightrope when improving quality of life through technological innovation, as novel hazards require cultural changes that are increasingly hard to coordinate. hyperstition (borrowing the term from ccru but inverting its valence) plays an important role: act as if a better world is already emerging by focusing mostly on the good. but this only works if grounded in verification & good faith — finding ways to check whether others share our goals even when their methods differ. without good faith we stop hyperstitioning; without verification of effort we will eventually make deadly mistakes; without technology we get wishful thinking. the simplest heuristic for shaping the world around us: reward what we like, and only punish what's actively working against the good. leave positive reviews. amplify good work. give attention to the things we value. energy flows where attention goes, and too many people waste theirs on outrage.
items.grounded: → combined with the rest of the above, you can slowly see why i might think it's worth working on diplomatic interventions.

items.title: the need for economic growth
items.summary: the average person today earns about $22,000/year in purchasing power. to bring everyone to swiss quality of life (~$82,000/year), global gdp needs to roughly quadruple — and that's before the cultural, educational, and infrastructure investment that maintains such quality of life. the real multiplier is thus probably higher. technological progress creates efficiencies: abundant nuclear energy, better materials, smarter logistics. the question how to grow sustainably, inclusively, and toward things that actually matter.
items.grounded: → why i think working on ai as the most consequential growth driver in history and getting it right matters more than anything.

items.title: limits to growth rates & maximum scale
items.summary: every entity — company, community, institution, movement — has a maximum growth rate it can sustain without losing coherence. it's similar to biological organisms that need to maintain homeostasis: grow too fast and something breaks, quality drops, culture erodes. there's also a maximum scale beyond which coordination costs exceed the value of coordination. even cities, which show superlinear returns to innovation, face diminishing returns across other dimensions — liveability, governance, social cohesion — following logistic curves that flatten. it's always a multi-objective optimization problem. still, we need to push the frontier of what's possible. staying small might feel safe but often means you stop getting feedback from reality about what's really possible and will eventually be outcompeted.
items.grounded: → combine this with bounded rationality and the need for growth, and we slowly get a cautious, human-scale, pro-growth framework.

items.title: aesthetics as coordination infrastructure
items.summary: we've over-optimized many things for cost-efficiency and lost something essential: the capacity to inspire awe. aesthetic grandeur — in architecture, interior design, art, fashion — is coordination infrastructure. beauty and awe connect people to their higher selves, to shared aspiration, to a sense that something larger is worth building toward. a future worth wanting needs to look and feel worth wanting. we need more inspiration and less baby beige. of course, we don't want pointless displays of wealth and negative sum status games, but minimalism also isn't the solution. and beauty becomes pretty intuitive with a little bit of training.
items.grounded: → maybe i'll be an industrial designer or architect one day.
